[2026-15181: lines 240-509 of 4520, FR page 47319]
   240  of the 60 investigations, certain acts, policies, and practices of the 
   241  economy at issue are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, 
   242  and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. Section 
   243  301(b) provides that upon determining that the acts, policies, and 
   244  practices under investigation are actionable and that action is 
   245  appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all appropriate and 
   246  feasible action authorized under Section 301(c), subject to the 
   247  specific direction, if any, of the President regarding such action, and 
   248  all other appropriate and feasible action within the power of the 
   249  President that the President may direct the Trade Representative to 
   250  take under Section 301(b), to obtain the elimination of that act, 
   251  policy, or practice. Section 301(b) provides further that actions 
   252  ``within the power of the President'' may include ``[a]ctions . . . 
   253  with respect to trade in any goods or services, or with respect to any 
   254  other area of pertinent relations with the foreign country.''
   255      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   256  to take certain, specific actions for purposes of carrying out the 
   257  provisions of Section 301(b). For example, Section 301(c)(1)(B) 
   258  authorizes the Trade Representative to ``impose duties or other import 
   259  restrictions on the goods'' of the foreign country subject to the 
   260  investigation. Section 301(c)(3)(A) provides that actions that the 
   261  Trade Representative is authorized to take may be taken against any 
   262  goods or economic sector on a non-discriminatory basis or solely 
   263  against the foreign country concerned. Section 301(c)(3)(B) empowers 
   264  the Trade Representative to take actions against any goods and economic 
   265  sector ``without regard to whether or not such goods or economic sector 
   266  were involved in the act, policy, or practice that is the subject of 
   267  such action.''
   268      USTR and the Section 301 Committee have carefully reviewed the 
   269  public comments and testimony regarding the proposed actions to be 
   270  taken in each investigation. The Trade Representative informed the 
   271  President of his recommended responsive actions in each investigation, 
   272  including, for each economy, whether to impose 10 or 12.5 percent 
   273  tariffs on all products of that economy or, in the case of specific 
   274  economies, 10 or 12.5 percent tariffs net of a product's MFN duty, with 
   275  exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative also informed 
   276  the President of economies that have imposed forced labor import 
   277  prohibitions, or undertaken commitments regarding forced labor import 
   278  prohibitions through an ART, since June 5, 2026. The Trade 
   279  Representative also advised the President that, after considering 
   280  significant comments and testimony on the proposed actions, certain 
   281  products warranted exemption from the tariffs imposed in the 
   282  investigations as they are: (a) raw materials that if subject to these 
   283  tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) 
   284  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these 
   285  tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
   286  quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained 
   287  from other sources; (d) products for which these tariffs may not be 
   288  effective in obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
   289  practices of economies found to be actionable in the investigations; or 
   290  (e) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El 
   291  Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   292  Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that would encourage these 
   293  economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import 
   294  prohibitions or to encourage these economies to enact and effectively 
   295  enforce a forced labor import prohibition.
   296      On July 23, 2026--after considering and taking account of the 
   297  information and advice provided by the Trade Representative; the 
   298  information, findings, and determinations in the June 5, 2026 FRN; the 
   299  need to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of 
   300  the investigated economies found to be actionable; and other pertinent 
   301  information--the President issued a memorandum (Memorandum) directing 
   302  that:
   303  
   304      Section 1. Tariffs and Exemptions. (a) Except as otherwise 
   305  provided in this memorandum, the Trade Representative shall impose 
   306  the following tariff rates on all goods of the economy for which an 
   307  act, policy, or
   308  
   309  [[Page 47320]]
   310  
   311  practice was found actionable under section 301:
   312      (i) 10 percent tariff rate: The Trade Representative shall 
   313  impose a tariff of 10 percent on goods of Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   314  Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, 
   315  Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United 
   316  Kingdom, and Trinidad and Tobago.
   317      (ii) Tariff rate of 10 percent or 12.5 percent, net of MFN rate: 
   318  For a product of the European Union or Taiwan, where such product's 
   319  MFN tariff is less than 10 percent, the Trade Representative shall 
   320  impose a section 301 tariff pursuant to these investigations so that 
   321  the sum of the MFN tariff and the section 301 tariff shall be 10 
   322  percent, and where such product's MFN tariff is greater than or 
   323  equal to 10 percent, the Trade Representative shall impose a section 
   324  301 tariff of zero. For a product of Japan, Korea, or Switzerland, 
   325  where such product's MFN tariff is less than 12.5 percent, the Trade 
   326  Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff pursuant to these 
   327  investigations so that the sum of the MFN tariff and the tariff 
   328  imposed pursuant to these investigations shall be 12.5 percent, and 
   329  where such product's MFN tariff is greater than or equal to 12.5 
   330  percent, the Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff 
   331  of zero. Capping total duties in this manner is feasible, consistent 
   332  with the terms of the Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar 
   333  arrangements, and appropriate to encourage these economies to 
   334  fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import prohibitions or to 
   335  enact and effectively enforce such a prohibition.
   336      (iii) 12.5 percent tariff rate: For goods of all other 
   337  investigated economies, the Trade Representative shall impose a 
   338  tariff rate of 12.5 percent.
   339      (b) The Trade Representative shall exempt from the tariffs 
   340  imposed as directed in subsection (a) of this section the products 
   341  identified in the Annex to this memorandum for each economy for 
   342  which an act, policy, or practice was found actionable under section 
   343  301, as the products identified constitute:
   344      (i) raw materials that if subject to these tariffs could lead to 
   345  the unavailability of domestic supply;
   346      (ii) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if 
   347  subject to these tariffs;
   348      (iii) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
   349  quantities in the United States or obtained from other sources;
   350      (iv) products for which these tariffs may not be effective in 
   351  obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of 
   352  economies found to be actionable in the investigations; or
   353      (v) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, 
   354  Ecuador, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, 
   355  Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that 
   356  would encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding 
   357  forced labor import prohibitions or to encourage these economies to 
   358  enact and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition.
   359      (c) After considering the relevant issues and factors and 
   360  weighing the relevant considerations, including potential economic 
   361  harm and efficacy of tariffs, I determine that the products 
   362  identified in the Annex to this memorandum shall be exempted from 
   363  the tariffs directed in subsection (a) of this section, and the 
   364  Trade Representative shall direct that the Harmonized Tariff 
   365  Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) be modified as provided in the 
   366  Annex to this memorandum. In my judgment, the tariffs directed in 
   367  subsection (a) of this section with the exemptions described in 
   368  subsection (b) of this section are appropriate and feasible to 
   369  obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, or practices of the 
   370  economies found to be actionable under section 301.
   371      Sec. 2. Tariff-Rate Quotas. (a) As soon as the Trade 
   372  Representative determines that it is feasible, the Trade 
   373  Representative shall:
   374      (i) establish TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and 
   375  Malaysia, with an initial duration of 3 years, to encourage the 
   376  importation by each of these economies of U.S. textile goods, in 
   377  order to reduce reliance on inputs from other sources that are more 
   378  likely to contain forced labor inputs; and
   379      (ii) structure the TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and 
   380  Malaysia to allow for a certain volume of specific textiles and 
   381  apparel, based on that economy's importation of U.S. inputs, to 
   382  enter the United States free of the section 301 tariffs provided for 
   383  in section 1(a) of this memorandum.
   384      (b) As soon as the Trade Representative determines that it is 
   385  feasible, the Trade Representative shall:
   386      (i) establish TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and 
   387  Malaysia, with an initial duration of 3 years, to encourage the 
   388  importation by each of these economies of U.S. cotton, in order to 
   389  reduce reliance on inputs from other sources that are more likely to 
   390  contain forced labor inputs; and
   391      (ii) structure the TRQs for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and 
   392  Malaysia to allow for a certain volume of specific textile and 
   393  apparel, based on that economy's importation of U.S. cotton, to 
   394  enter the United States free of the section 301 tariffs provided for 
   395  in section 1(a) of this memorandum.
   396      (c) Until the Trade Representative establishes the TRQs 
   397  described in subsections (a) and (b) of this section, the Trade 
   398  Representative shall impose the applicable section 301 tariffs 
   399  provided for in section 1(a) of this memorandum (here, 10 percent) 
   400  on imports of specific textile and apparel of Bangladesh, Cambodia, 
   401  Indonesia, and Malaysia that will be covered by the TRQs for each of 
   402  those economies.
   403      (d) The Trade Representative shall modify the HTSUS as 
   404  appropriate to implement the directives in this section. The Trade 
   405  Representative shall publish a notice in the Federal Register 
   406  regarding the establishment and the effective date of the TRQs 
   407  directed in this section.
   408  
   409      The Memorandum further directs that in the President's judgment, 
   410  tariffs for each economy of 10 or 12.5 percent on all goods or, in the 
   411  case of specific economies, 10 or 12.5 percent net of a good's MFN 
   412  duty, with the exemptions described in the Memorandum, are appropriate 
   413  and feasible to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
   414  practices of each economy found to be actionable under Section 301. 
   415  With respect to the tariff actions and exemptions, the Memorandum also 
   416  states the President's determination that alternatives to the action 
   417  directed by the President, such as a lower tariff rate, negotiation 
   418  without the imposition of tariffs, action under other statutory 
   419  authority without action under Section 301 of the Trade Act, and 
   420  combinations of various approaches, would be less effective and less 
   421  preferable than the action directed in the Memorandum.
   422      Considering the public comments and testimony and the advice of the 
   423  Section 301 Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, 
   424  and pursuant to Sections 301(b) and 304(a) of the Trade Act, the Trade 
   425  Representative has determined that action is appropriate in each 
   426  investigation. In accordance with the specific direction of the 
   427  President, and considering the public comments and testimony, the 
   428  advice of the Section 301 Committee, as well as the advice of advisory 
   429  committees, the Trade Representative has determined pursuant to 
   430  Sections 301(b), 301(c), and 304(a) of the Trade Act that appropriate 
   431  and feasible action in each investigation is the application of tariffs 
   432  to all imports of the investigated economy at issue, with certain 
   433  exemptions detailed in Annexes I and II to this Notice.
   434      With respect to tariff rates, the Trade Representative has 
   435  determined, consistent with the specific direction of the President, to

I'm going through the proposed tariff rates by country: 10% flat for a list of countries including Canada, the EU, Mexico and the UK, and 12.5% for everyone else. I'm checking how Switzerland and Norway come out under that, since their figures are being netted against MFN.

I'm checking the remaining country rates against their net-of-MFN figures: the UK and Taiwan come out at 10, Türkiye and Hong Kong stay at 12.5, and Japan and Germany shift once MFN is netted. India is the one whose rate changed, going from 12.5 to 10. Next I'm running the Q6 totals country by country, starting with Switzerland's 8.5% net and Norway's flat 12.5%.

I'm working through the totals for the remaining countries: Japan's 0.5% MFN gap works out to $500, Liechtenstein isn't an investigated economy so it contributes nothing, and India comes to $10,000 and a $14,000 total. I'm also checking that Norway isn't netted against MFN, and that Germany and Taiwan get no extra MFN-based reduction.

I'm checking Korea's figures next: at an MFN rate of 10%, the gap to 12.5% is 2.5%, or $2,500. Switzerland's duty-free case comes to the full 12.5%, or $12,500. I'm also noting that Korea was at a flat 12.5% in the June proposal, so I'll keep that in mind. After that I'll move on to Q7 and look for how the non-ad valorem MFN rates are handled, starting with the "ad valorem equivalent" wording in the notice.

content.text:
I just realized Canada is covered by the Section 301 action, with a 10% tariff under heading 9903.05.29 and an exemption for goods that qualify under USMCA. That matters for Q10 on Canadian goods in September 2026, since the duty actually applies to them. For part (d), the question gives a 10% Section 301 duty on the rye whisky, which comes to $6,000 without a USMCA claim, so I'm now working out what the figure becomes when the USMCA claim is made.

I'm checking the Section 301 exemptions for the Q15 Canadian goods, where 232 articles come out at zero. Then I'm running the Q9 figures: the 9802.00.80 assembly duty on $65,000 at Thailand's 12.5% comes to $8,125, and the 9802.00.50 repair duty on $6,000 at Israel's 12.5% comes to $750. I'm now on the Mexico part (c).

I'm checking Mexico under 9903.05.55 next: the USMCA-qualifying goods come out at zero, and the non-qualifying part at 10% of $50,000, or $5,000, with the MFN rate kept separate. For Japan's passenger car under 9903.94.01, the exemption in (f)(2) brings the duty to zero. Then there's Brazil's 232 case: the adopted exemption list names specific headings, and this one isn't among them, so I'm treating it as not exempt, which would put the 12.5% duty at $12,500, though I want to check whether the broader exemption language I recall applies.

I'm checking the passage on informational materials and donations to see whether it's part of the adopted exemptions, so I'll read the next section before deciding.

content.text:
I'm working through the non-ad valorem MFN rule for Q7(d), checking the U.S. note 52(k) provisions for the EU member states, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan. I'm also looking at the headings text for 9903.05.39 and 9903.05.76 to see how the 10 percent cap applies when the column 1 rate is below that level.

I'm working out the Q7 numbers: for France the specific duty comes to about 0.5% ad valorem, leaving a 9.5% cap gap worth $1,140, and for Italy the column 1 duty works out to 9%, so the EU cap leaves 1%, or $200. I'm also checking Japan, Brazil, Taiwan, and Switzerland against their caps, and then I'll go back to whether note (k) covers the specific-rate case.

I'm checking the patented pharmaceutical exemption in the amended heading 9903.05.90, which takes effect July 31, 2026. For the Q8 Dominican Republic shipments, the July 30 entry falls before that cutoff, so the 12.5 percent Section 301 duty still applies, and the August 3 entry is exempt.

I'm going through the Dominican Republic shipments one by one against the July 24 and July 28 cutoffs for the in-transit exception. The July 29 entry falls outside the window, and the July 27 entry gets in before the July 28 cutoff, so it's exempt. The July 28 12:01 am and July 24 6:00 am loadings also miss their cutoffs and owe the full $10,000.

I'm working through the air freight shipment, which was loaded onto an aircraft in Santo Domingo and flown directly to Miami. The in-transit exception text only names vessels, so I'm checking whether the Annex language covers air transport at all before deciding if that entry owes the full $10,000.

I'm going to search the source for any note that mentions "in transit" to see whether the Annex covers the in-transit exception for non-vessel modes.

content.text:
I'm checking the memo's recitals against the June proposal. The memo calls the textile mechanism a zero Section 301 rate, but the June notice says "reduced," so that's a discrepancy worth flagging as a Q11 item. I'm also starting to look at the proposed 10% ad valorem tariffs on goods from certain economies.

I'm now comparing the memo's list of economies that impose a forced labor import ban but don't yet enforce it, and I'm also noting that the memo cites notice number 2026-11296. I'm seeing that the memo's (d) and (e) labels look swapped relative to the notice, which is minor. I'm also checking the tariff rates: Cambodia was already at 10% in the June proposal, so the memo's claim that seven economies moved from 12.5% to 10% looks wrong, and I think five economies actually moved.

I'm confirming that Honduras wasn't in the June 12.5% group, so it moved down to 10%, which makes the memo's count of five economies moving (not seven) accurate on that point. Cambodia and Guatemala were already at 10% in the June proposal, and Jordan's change came from an ART commitment rather than a ban.

Checking the memo's Honduras and Taiwan treatment next: the memo says Taiwan was proposed at 10% but adopted net of MFN under a 10% cap. I'm also noting that Ecuador and Indonesia show up in both the forced labor ban list and the ART list in June, and that the memo's recitals about the six non-enforcing economies match the June notice.

I'm now checking whether the memo's section 1(b) lettering matches the notice, and I'm also weighing whether the memo's statement about Trade Representative timing for TRQs is a real discrepancy or just a reported recital.

I'm checking the memo's section 2(c) wording against how the notice quotes it, including the "(here, 10 percent)" parenthetical, so I'll read that part of the memo directly.

I'm checking the memo's section 4(e) wording on applicable tariff actions and finding it consistent. The memo doesn't say anything about in-transit goods or foreign trade zones, and the dates line comes from USTR instead. I'm also confirming that the section 3(b) tariff of 10 percent on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia looks fine, and now I'm turning to the other key items I still need to cover.

Next I need the exemption details in sections III.C through E of the notice, so I'm going to scan that part for the key figures on beef, avocados, sugar, and the 12.5 percent cap.

content.text:
I'm checking the quiz answers: item 4 was marked wrong, since beef and avocados stayed exempt after opposition comments tied them to forced labor and USTR declined to remove them. For item 10, the line about only certain chemicals being cut back looks right, though the exact wording is "except the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products." I also want to see whether Annex A covered all articles and parts under Section 232, because the proposed and adopted versions seem to differ there.

I'm now checking whether the adopted notice's treatment of Section 232 articles matches what the June proposal said about Annex A, since the two documents seem to describe that exemption differently. The adopted text limits the 232 exemption to enumerated headings, which may or may not count as a cut back, so I'm weighing that against the notice's claim that it exempted all proposed products except the non-pharmaceutical chemicals.

I'm checking the 471-product sugar claim against the notice, which lists only "certain" sugar and sugar-containing products rather than all of them, so that part of the quiz answer looks wrong. I'll also check item 7's statement about the notice.

I'm checking the 12.5% cap claim next, since the net-of-MFN caps seem to apply only to the EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, with other economies getting 12.5 added on top of MFN. I'm also comparing which economies have their own negotiated exempt-product list, because Japan and Korea don't appear to have one.

I'm checking whether Japan's section also limits its exemption to Annex I and Annex II, Part A, the way Korea's does at line 1155, so I'll look at the lines around the Japan provisions to confirm.

I'm checking the reasons for India's classification and noting that the EU's 10 percent figure is net of MFN. For question 6(c), I'm comparing Switzerland, Japan, and Germany, with Switzerland and Japan both at 12.5 percent net of MFN.

Next I'm checking the EU and Taiwan, both at 10 percent net of MFN, and India dropping to 10 because its ban was adopted after June 5. Norway, the UK, Türkiye and Hong Kong stay as they are, and Liechtenstein wasn't investigated. Then I'll look for any later USTR notices on the textile TRQ, and check the Cambodia exemptions in the notes for the relevant HTS codes.

content.text:
Now I'm checking question 12 part (a): the aloe-type product at $60,000 is exempt for Cambodia, so that leg is zero, but Malaysia's list doesn't include aloe, which means a 10% duty on the $60,000. Then I'm moving to part (b) on the boswellia product at $100,000, which is exempt under Malaysia's list.

Now I'm working through parts (b) through (e) of question 12, checking each product against the exemption lists for the listed economies. For (d), the sesame seeds are exempt everywhere under the note, so each economy comes out to zero. For (e), the psyllium husks are exempt only for Cambodia, so Thailand, El Salvador, and Italy each carry a duty.

Weighing whether the EU leg of Q12(e) should be added, I'm settling on 8% of $40,000, or $3,200. I'm also noting that the heading numbers matter for the Canada and Section 301 rates, then turning to Q13 and the Section 232 proclamation changes for aluminum, steel, and copper, with the June 2026 and April 2026 proclamations still to be searched.

I'm noting a July 2026 notice on further aluminum import adjustments, which may matter for the aluminum extrusion questions, Q13 and Q15. content.text:
I'm working through Q13, an Annex I-C machine, where the 25% rate runs from June 8, 2026 through the end of December 31, 2027. For the Canadian USMCA case with $60,000 of US parts, I'm calculating the non-US content at 140,000, which comes to $35,000 at 25%, giving an effective rate of 17.5%.

I'm now checking the remaining cases: a Canadian part with no US content gives 25% on the full $200,000, and a non-USMCA Canadian case also comes to $50,000. For the Japan case, I'm taking the 2.5% MFN off the 15% total to get 12.5%, or $25,000. The aluminum smelted in the US inside a Canadian part doesn't count as US-produced parts, so I'm settling that case at $45,000.

I'm checking whether the October 6 date matters, since it may relate to the July proclamation or a later rule change, so I'll grep the documents for the relevant dates and the proclamation text.

For (g), the non-US content is $60,000 at 25%, which is $15,000, or 7.5% of the $200,000 total; the 15% floor then sets the duty at $30,000. I'm now checking (a), which I'm working out as $35,000 at 17.5%.

I'm checking the remaining questions: (b) is USMCA with no US content, so 25% on $200,000 gives $50,000, and the Section 301 question doesn't apply since only Section 232 is in play. Next I need the historical chain for Q15, covering the Canada IEEPA orders, the aluminum Section 232 proclamations and their effective dates, and the later changes to IEEPA.

I'm going to search for a court ruling that ends the IEEPA tariffs, checking for any related terminations involving Canada.

I'm working out the surcharge window, which runs from Feb 24, 2026 through July 24, 2026, and I'm noting that 232 aluminum goods and USMCA-covered goods are excluded. For the March 2 entry, the aluminum is under 232 at 50%, so Section 122 isn't owed, and I'm checking whether the clause that stops the surcharge on 232 portions applies to the full value here.

Now I'm looking at how the IEEPA Canada duties were ended, and I think a February 2026 executive order titled "Ending Certain Tariff Actions" may have done it. I'll search for that order and any related Federal Register notice dated from February 1, 2026 onward.

content.text:
I'm checking whether the order has an effective date, and the text only says it stops being in effect and gets collected as soon as practicable. I'm weighing whether the end date falls on Feb 24, but that doesn't matter for the Q15 dates I need.

I'm now working through the Q15 dates one by one, starting with Feb 10, 2025. EO 14193 was signed Feb 1 and took effect Feb 4, but the pause under EO 14197 holds the IEEPA duties until March 4, so nothing additional applies on Feb 10. I'm also checking whether the 2018 Section 232 aluminum duties still touched Canada then, since Canada was exempted from them.

I'm now going through the March dates, starting with March 6, 2025. The 25% IEEPA duty applies to both cases that day, since the USMCA exemption only takes effect March 7, so that comes to $25,000 each. On March 10, the non-USMCA case still pays $25,000, but the USMCA case is exempt by then and pays nothing.

I'm working through the stacking question for March 14, 2025: the 25% Section 232 aluminum duty from March 12 would add $25,000 on both cases, and I need to check whether the Executive Order from April 29 changes how the IEEPA duties on Canadian goods combine with it.

I'm checking whether the 232 steel and aluminum duties stack with the IEEPA duties on Canadian goods under the April 29 order. I think that order bars stacking for autos, and I'm not sure whether it covers steel and aluminum too.

I'm checking whether the 232 steel and aluminum duties on Canadian goods stack with the IEEPA duties, and whether the stacking order mentions them or only autos. I'm not certain the April 29 order covers steel and aluminum, so I'm leaving that open.

I'm checking whether the 25% Section 232 steel and aluminum duty stacks with the Canada IEEPA duty on March 14, 2025. Case N would pay $25,000 under each, so $50,000 in total, while Case U would pay $25,000 under 232 with no IEEPA duty on top.

I'm planning to confirm whether the 2025 aluminum Section 232 proclamation is in the database, and whether the stacking order and the March amendments change anything for March 14. I have a limited research budget, so I'll make targeted searches before settling the answer.

I'm going to make a few quick checks on the research budget before settling the answer.

content.text:
I'm checking whether the IEEPA tariff order applies on top of the Section 232 aluminum duties, and I'm wondering whether Canadian goods are actually excluded from the reciprocal tariffs under that order, so I need to verify that against the text.

I'm checking the Canada exclusion in EO 14257 by searching its text, and I'm working out the tariff stacking for Q15 across the dated cases. For non-USMCA goods the totals come to 85,000 after August 5, 2025, and for USMCA goods they come to 50,000, since the aluminum duty still applies while IEEPA does not.

Now I'm checking the March 2 and June 10, 2026 dates, where Section 232 still sets the rate at 50% under Annex I-A, so each of those totals comes to 50,000. Section 122 doesn't stack on top because 232 goods are excluded from it, and USMCA goods are exempt from it too. July 27, 2026 looks the same, with the 232 duty at 50%.

I'm now checking the July 24 cutoff, since the Section 122 surcharge lapses then and the Section 301 Canada duty exempts aluminum articles under the 9903.82.02 provision, so the total stays at 50,000. Section 338 isn't in effect until August 22, so it doesn't change the total. For August 25 and September 14, the Section 232 duty is still 50%, and Section 338 and Section 301 both fall away for articles already under 232, leaving 50,000 in each case.

I'm checking the September 16, 2026 case, where Section 232 still gives 50,000 and the Section 338 duty adds another 50% on the 100,000 base, bringing the total to 100,000. I'm unsure whether Section 338 reaches USMCA-qualifying goods, since the annex that might exempt them is unreadable, so I'm flagging that point for verification.

I'm now checking the November 10, 2026 case, where Section 232 gives 50,000 and Section 338 adds another 50,000, so the total is 100,000, since the October scope proclamation doesn't touch extrusions. For Case U, Annex I-A applies rather than I-C, so the 50% rate holds on the full value with no USMCA content provision. I'm also going back to February 10, 2025, to see whether the 232 aluminum duty on Canadian goods was already exempt by then.

I'm checking the March 2026 dates and the Canada reciprocal-tariff question next, starting with whether Canadian goods fall outside the reciprocal tariffs entirely.

content.text:
I'm checking the Canadian goods case for September 2026 entries. The reciprocal tariff doesn't apply to them, since the steel and aluminum goods are excluded and Canada is carved out under (d). Next I'm looking at whether the IEEPA basis and the 10% surcharge still reach those entries, given the executive order that ended IEEPA and the proclamation that let the surcharge lapse in July.

Now I'm working through the Canadian rye whisky case for September entries: the section 338 duty at 50% on the $60,000 would be $30,000, and the USMCA claim would drop the section 301 duty to zero. Without that claim, the 301 duty at 10% adds $6,000, bringing the total to $36,000. For an October 2 arrival, the import ban applies, so no duty is owed and the goods can't be entered at all.

Now I'm weighing the Sept 10 extrusion entry against the Sept 16 one: the 232 duty at 50% applies either way, but the section 338 duty only starts once the scope proclamation takes effect on the 15th, so the earlier entry gets no 338 duty.

Now I'm checking the Annex II alcohol entries (X, Y, Z) at 25% under Section 232, each on $100,000 full value, and whether Section 338 applies to them for September 10 entries. The clause exempting articles already subject to 232 duties means Section 338 doesn't add anything for those three.

I'm checking the October 1 entry for the X alcohol goods: the scope proclamation makes the 338 duty at 50% apply on top of the 25% Section 232 duty, so that's $50,000 plus $25,000, or $75,000 total.

I'm confirming that the dairy entry has no scope proclamation, so clause (2) of 11047 still applies and the section 338 duty is zero, leaving just the 25% Section 232 duty of $25,000. For the motor vehicle goods, the scope proclamation's clause (1) makes the 338 duty apply, so that's $50,000 on top of the $25,000 Section 232 duty.

I'm checking whether the exclusion proclamation changes the duty on listed Canadian alcohol not in its annex, and it doesn't, since the text says it leaves those duties as they are and the 50% rate still applies. For the FTZ case, the September 25 arrival was imported before the ban date, so the 50% duty of $15,000 still applies on the October 6 consumption entry, though the text doesn't address FTZ directly, so I'm flagging that.

I'm now going through the wine entries and the imports that arrive just after the 12:01 a.m. cutoff on September 29. Any goods that come in at that point are excluded from importation and can't be entered, so no duty applies to them.

I'm now checking the 12:01 a.m. August 22 cutoff for the wine entries: the 2:00 p.m. August 20 and 11:59 p.m. August 21 entries fall before it, so no duty applies, while the 12:01 a.m. August 22 entry carries a 50% duty on $40,000, or $20,000. I'm also going back over how the amendment works, since the chapeau of Annex II is changed to read August 22 while the proclamation's numbered clauses and preamble still print August 19.

I'm checking how the amendment sets the August 22 effective date, since the proclamation's numbered clauses and preamble still print August 19 while the chapeau of Annex II is changed. The later documents confirm duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. on August 22, and the September scope documents repeat August 19 in their recitals, which I'm noting as a discrepancy. I'm also considering whether clause (2) of the original proclamation suspends collection or merely postpones the effective date, and I'm starting to look at the refund provision in clause (4).

I'm checking the refund clause for the August 22 wine entry, which only says refunds follow standard CBP procedures, with no special amount or timing. The suspension was signed August 18 and published after that entry, and I'm also noting that Canada reneged on August 21 so the duties took effect automatically at 12:01 a.m. on August 22.

I'm double-checking the reasoning on the August 22 wine entry's refund and the timing of the suspension, and noting that the recitals describe a "3-day suspension" even though the operative text changes the effective date. I'm also starting to count the days from July 20 to August 19 to confirm the 30-day window.

I'm working out the timing of the 30-day waiting period for section 338. Counted from the July 20 signing date, Aug 19 is 30 days out, but counted from the July 23 publication date, it lands on Aug 22, which matches the postponed effective date. I also need to check how the September scope proclamations describe their own 30-day wait for the two cases I'm tracking.

Now I'm working out the 30-day timing for section 338: counted from the July 20 signing, August 19 falls exactly 30 days later, which matches the earlier date, but counted from the July 23 publication, it lands on August 22, the actual start. The text doesn't say which count controls, so I'll show both. I'm also planning a table of the entry dates and the proclamations that govern each.

Now I'm lining up the key dates for each proclamation: the August 22 effective date for the alcohol duties, the September 29 import ban keyed to arrival, and the September 15 and October 30 entry-based cutoffs. I'm also noting which product groups each one covers, with alcohol under the original proclamation, the delay, and the later ban, and dairy under its own line.

Now I'm cross-checking the Federal Register first pages for each proclamation and noting the Annex II and dairy treatment, with the Section 232 stacking on the motor vehicle goods. I'm also looking at the 11076 timing, which was signed October 23 and filed October 29.

Now I'm checking the October 30 scope proclamation: it was published the same day it applied, and it reaches only entries made on or after that date. Neither scope proclamation has a refund clause, so I'm treating the August refund provision as the only one that covers this. I'm also turning to which Part of 11065 makes goods subject to the duty and which one releases them.

Now I'm checking the motor vehicle scope dates for the September and October proclamations, and confirming which parts of the annex apply to the goods in question. I'm also noting that the July memorandum was signed July 23 and published July 28, even though its duties applied from 12:01 a.m. on July 24, so the duties took effect before publication.

Now I'm applying the July 28 cutoff to the entries: the first is dutiable at $10,000, the July 27 entry at 3 p.m. is exempt, and the 12:01 a.m. July 28 entry is dutiable too. I'm also checking the July 24 loading entry and the pharma exclusion from July 31, where the July 30 entry still carries the 12.5% duty on $80,000.

I'm checking the Dominican Republic 12.5% rate against the listing on page 47323, then moving to the Israel repair entry, where the duty applies only to the value of the repairs. For the Mexico entry, I'm treating the USMCA-qualifying goods as exempt under note 52(h), and I'm starting to work out the 10% figure on the second Mexican item.

Now I'm checking the Brazil entry, where the note exempts only the headings it lists, so the general 12.5% applies and the 232 stacking sits on top. I'm also checking the June proposal's wording on goods already under section 232, informational materials, and accompanied baggage.

I'm going to search the 15181 text for "informational" and "donation" to see whether the informational materials and donations exemptions from the June proposal made it into the final note 52, since the annex text may carry them instead.

content.text:
I'm checking whether the adopted readable text has any informational materials or donations exemption, since that may sit in an annex list instead. The reference to headings 9903.05.85 through 9903.06.21 in note 52(a) is unclear to me, so I'm leaving that open. For now I'll treat the readable text as silent on this and look at the notice's own recital next.

I'm now weighing a possible discrepancy on the 232 exemptions. The June notice says Annex A covers all 232 articles, while the other notice separates informational materials and 232 articles from the Annex A products, and its claim about exempting all Annex A products doesn't match the specific 232 headings in the adopted note 52(f). I'll note that and check the textile mechanism recital next.

I'm now comparing the memo's description of the textile mechanism, which says "zero section 301 tariff rate," against the June notice's "reduced" rate, and the adopted text's "free of the section 301 tariffs," which suggests the memo misdescribes the proposal. I'm also questioning whether listing Cambodia and Guatemala at the 10 percent rate implies a change, since they were already at that level in the proposal. That one seems only moderately significant.

Now I'm going through the remaining candidate discrepancies: the weak ordering difference in the exemption categories, the TRQ timing language that doesn't actually conflict, and whether the pharmaceutical limitation matches what the June proposal said.

I'm checking the Federal Register notice's footnote-style points on Canada, where the August proclamation sets the effective date at August 19 while a later one moves the Annex II change to August 22 and leaves the other clauses in place. I'm also noting that the FTZ privileged-status language ties to when the additional duty takes effect, and that the Switzerland rate in the notice matches the exempt list in note 52(j)(3).

I'm now looking at the Canada proclamations, where the August 19 effective date in the first one seems to be changed to August 22 by a later one that amends only the Annex II language. The September proclamations still describe the duties as effective August 19, which may be inaccurate given that amendment.

I'm now checking the Canada proclamations again: the 11056 text describes a three-day "suspension" of duties that hadn't yet taken effect when it was signed, and the September proclamations still recite an August 19 effective date despite the later change to August 22. I'm also comparing Saskatchewan's treatment in 11061 against the earlier proclamation's description of provincial bans.

I'm now checking the Canada proclamations against each other: 11046 says Alberta and Saskatchewan later lifted their provincial bans in June 2025, but 11061 describes Saskatchewan as not having outright banned imports, which doesn't match. I'm also looking at the dairy TRQ language in 11062 and the "effective August 19" recital in 11076 and 11065, and I'm about to compare the Part A clause in 11064 and 11065.

I'm checking the Canada proclamations for how the August 19 effective date shifts and whether the 11056 "suspension" and the provincial ban descriptions line up with each other. I'm also noting that the next part is about how one proclamation describes the scope of the duty and a ban that the others characterize differently.

I'm checking whether the 11046 proclamation actually states that Canada's imposition is "not equally enforced" the way the later proclamations describe it, since its finding seems to be worded differently. The later recitals in 11056 and 11061 add that phrase, but 11046's own finding doesn't include it, so the descriptions may not match.

I'm now checking the alcohol proclamations against 11046's own finding, which says Canada's imposition is unreasonable and discriminating but doesn't use "not equally enforced." The later recitals in 11056 and 11061 add that phrase, so their description of 11046 looks inaccurate.

I'm checking whether the scope proclamation's "no longer subject" language conflicts with the 50 percent rate in clause (2) for products that sit in both the ban annex and alcohol Part B, though that may depend on the annex images. I'm also comparing the notice's summary of the 10 percent rate with the 12.5 percent rate applied to Japan, Korea, and Switzerland, which seems to be the next point.

I'm now checking the Notice's own statement that all sixty investigated economies failed both the prohibition and enforcement factors, since its earlier section says only fifty-four failed to impose and enforce and six failed only on enforcement. Those two counts don't agree with the "all 60" line, so I'm marking that as an internal inconsistency in the notice.

I'm going to check the June Federal Register notice's own determinations against how this notice describes them, since the "all 60 failed both factors" line doesn't match the six economies that only failed on enforcement. I'll pull up that section of the June notice to compare the counts directly.

Q1.answer:
Ten documents, all signed by the President. Dates are 2026. 'Applies' means the operative change.

1. Proc. 11046 (alcohol duty), FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46639. Signed Jul 20, published Jul 23. It imposes a 50% duty on Annex II products. Applies 12:01 a.m. ET Aug 19 (later moved to Aug 22 by Proc. 11056), measured against goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption.
2. Proc. 11047 (dairy duty), 2026-14992, 91 FR 46653. Same dates and same event as 11046.
3. Proc. 11048 (motor-vehicles duty), 2026-14997, 91 FR 46663. Same dates and same event as 11046.
4. Proc. 11056 (3-day delay), 2026-17294, 91 FR 54789. Signed Aug 18, filed Aug 21, published Aug 24. Clause (1) sets the effective date of 11046, 11047 and 11048 at 12:01 a.m. ET Aug 22. This is still measured against entry or warehouse withdrawal.
5. Proc. 11061 (alcohol import ban), 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311. Signed Sep 8, published Sep 14. Applies 12:01 a.m. Sep 29, measured against importation (arrival), not entry.
6. Proc. 11062 (dairy ban), 2026-18836, 91 FR 58319. Same dates and same event as 11061.
7. Proc. 11063 (motor-vehicles ban), 2026-18837, 91 FR 58325. Same dates and same event as 11061.
8. Proc. 11064 (alcohol scope), 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331. Signed Sep 8, published Sep 14. Applies 12:01 a.m. Sep 15, measured against entry or warehouse withdrawal.
9. Proc. 11065 (motor-vehicles scope), 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339. Same dates and same event as 11064.
10. Proc. 11076 (further motor-vehicles scope), 2026-22292, 91 FR 68861. Signed Oct 23, filed Oct 29, published Oct 30. Applies 12:01 a.m. Oct 30, measured against entry or warehouse withdrawal.

Products affected, by group:
- Alcohol: 11046 puts the Annex II products under the duty. 11056 delays the start. 11064 adds Part A products and removes Part B products from the duty. 11061 bans the products in its Annex from importation on or after Sep 29. Goods imported earlier stay dutiable.
- Dairy: 11047 imposes the duty. 11056 delays it. 11062 bans the products in its Annex. No dairy scope proclamation exists.
- Motor vehicles: 11048 imposes the duty. 11056 delays it. 11065 adds Part A products and removes Part B products. 11063 bans the products in its Annex. 11076 reverses the labels: Part A leaves the duty and Part B becomes dutiable.
Q1.basis: Operative clauses: 11046 cl.(1) at 91 FR 46641. 11047 cl.(1) at 46654. 11048 cl.(1) at 46665. 11056 cl.(1) at 54790. 11061, 11062 and 11063 cl.(1)-(3) at 58312, 58320 and 58326. 11064 cl.(1) at 58332. 11065 cl.(1) at 58340. 11076 cl.(1) at 68862. Signing, filing and publication dates come from the FR headers and filing stamps. Searches by title and by 'Canadian discrimination' returned exactly these ten documents.
Q1.uncertainty: Annex contents (which products are on each list) are images, so product-level changes cannot be read. 11056 delays the start without describing it as an amendment of the numbered clauses. No later document through Nov 14, 2026 was found.

Q2.answer:
(a) Entry 1 (2:00 p.m. Aug 20): $0. Entry 2 (11:59 p.m. Aug 21): $0. Entry 3 (12:01 a.m. Aug 22): 50% × $40,000 = $20,000. The duty applies to goods entered or withdrawn on or after 12:01 a.m. ET Aug 22. The controlling text is Proc. 11056 cl.(1), read with 11046 cl.(1).

(b) 11056 cl.(1) says the effective date 'shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026'. It then amends only 'the chapeau of Annex II' of each of 11046, 11047 and 11048, replacing 'August 19, 2026' with 'August 22, 2026'. The Annex II chapeau is an image. The numbered clauses (1) and (3) of 11046 and the preamble paragraph 9 were not amended and still print Aug 19. The conflict is resolved by 11056 cl.(1)'s own date statement and by cl.(5), which supersedes inconsistent provisions of earlier proclamations. Later proclamations confirm that the duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. Aug 22 (11061 ¶4).

(c) 11056 cl.(4) says that 'to the extent' implementation requires a refund of duties collected, refunds 'shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures'. It gives no special mechanism, deadline or amount. Entry 1 predates Aug 22, so no duty was owed on it and the deposit is refundable under that clause.

(d) No. The duties began automatically at 12:01 a.m. Aug 22. 11061 ¶4 says 'the 3-day suspension imposed by Proclamation 11056 lapsed, and the additional ad valorem duties ... became effective'. 11061 ¶2-3 say the following. On Aug 18, 11056 delayed the start for 3 days after Canada expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination. On Aug 21, Canada 'reneged on its commitment'.

(e) The original start date is the signing date plus 30 days: Jul 20 + 11 days = Jul 31, and Jul 31 + 19 days = Aug 19, a total of 30 days. 11046 ¶10 recites that section 338 duties may not 'take effect earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation'.
Q2.uncertainty: The text does not say whether the 30 days run from signing or from publication. July 23 (publication) + 30 days = Aug 22, which is the date actually used. 11056 was filed Aug 21 and published Aug 24, after the new start. The wording of the Annex II chapeau cannot be read.

Q3.answer:
(a) A. Arrives Sep 10 and entered Sep 14: it was imported before Sep 29, so the ban does not apply. The 50% duty applies: 50% × $30,000 = $15,000 (MFN free, so no other layer).
B. Arrives Sep 27, withdrawn from warehouse Oct 5: it was imported before Sep 29 but entered or withdrawn afterwards. It 'remain[s] subject to the 50 percent duty': $15,000.
C. Arrives 11:30 p.m. Sep 28 and entered 9:00 a.m. Sep 29: imported before 12:01 a.m. Sep 29, so it remains dutiable at $15,000.
D. Arrives 12:30 a.m. Sep 29: imported after the cutoff, so it is excluded from importation. It may not be imported or entered, and no 338 duty is assessed.

(b) Shipment E arrived Sep 25, before Sep 29, so it is not banned. It was admitted to the FTZ in privileged foreign status (11046 cl.(4)). On entry for consumption on Oct 6 the 50% duty applies: $15,000. The ban text addresses imports and warehouse withdrawals, not FTZ withdrawals.

(c) If the ban is invalidated as to an import, 11061 cl.(9)(b) says 'the 50 percent ad valorem duty imposed in Proclamation 11046 shall apply to the import' (50% × $30,000 = $15,000 per shipment). The duty applies to imports to which the invalidated ban had applied.

(d) No. 11061 cl.(3) says that besides moving products from the duty to the ban, the proclamation 'does not otherwise affect' which products are subject to the 11046 duties. Listed alcoholic products not in the ban Annex stay subject to the 50% duty as modified by 11064.
Q3.uncertainty: The ban's treatment of FTZ goods is not stated. Treating FTZ admission as 'imported' before Sep 29 is the most defensible reading. Annex contents are images. 11061 cl.(2) says goods remain at 50% even if the 11064 scope change removed them from the duty, but the product lists cannot be read.

Q4.answer:
(a) Entries Sep 10, 2026 ($100,000 each):
- X (alcohol): section 232 = 25% × $100,000 = $25,000. Section 338 = $0.
- Y (dairy): section 232 = $25,000. Section 338 = $0.
- Z (motor vehicles): section 232 = $25,000. Section 338 = $0.
The original proclamations exclude articles subject to section 232 from the 338 duty. The scope proclamations that reverse this start Sep 15.

(b) Entries Oct 1, 2026:
- X: section 232 = $25,000. Section 338 = 50% × $100,000 = $50,000. Total $75,000.
- Y: section 232 = $25,000. Section 338 = $0, because no dairy scope proclamation exists and 11047 cl.(2) still excludes 232 articles. Total $25,000.
- Z: section 232 = $25,000. Section 338 = $50,000. Total $75,000.

(c) Deciding text:
- 11046 cl.(2) at 91 FR 46641, 11047 cl.(2) at 46655 and 11048 cl.(2) at 46665 each say: 'The duties imposed in this proclamation shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232 ...'.
- 11064 cl.(1) at 58332 and 11065 cl.(1) at 58340 each say: 'The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046 [11048], as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232 ...', effective for entries on or after 12:01 a.m. Sep 15, 2026.
Q4.uncertainty: The scope proclamations' stacking sentence is written about the duty 'as modified' and appears in the clause that deals with Part A and Part B lists. I read it as covering every product still dutiable, including products on neither Part. The Annex I exceptions to the original proclamations cannot be read.

Q5.answer:
(a) Does the 50% duty apply? Times in order: Sep 14 3:00 p.m. / Sep 15 12:01 a.m. / Oct 29 4:00 p.m. / Oct 30 12:01 a.m. / Nov 3.
- P: No / Yes / Yes / Yes / Yes. Part A of the September proclamation makes it dutiable from Sep 15 12:01 a.m. The October proclamation does not touch it.
- Q: Yes / No / No / No / No. It was dutiable under the original Annex II from Aug 22. September Part B removes it from Sep 15 12:01 a.m.
- R: Yes / Yes / Yes / No / No. It was dutiable from Aug 22. The September proclamation does not touch it. October Part A removes it from Oct 30 12:01 a.m.
- S: No / No / No / Yes / Yes. October Part B makes it dutiable from Oct 30 12:01 a.m.
In the September proclamation (11065) Part A means 'shall be subject' and Part B means 'no longer subject'. In October (11076) the labels are reversed.

(b) Proclamation 11076: signed Oct 23, 2026; filed with the Office of the Federal Register Oct 29 (11:15 a.m.); published Oct 30 (91 FR 68861); applies from 12:01 a.m. ET Oct 30. Neither scope proclamation reaches earlier entries, because each applies only to goods entered or withdrawn on or after its time. Neither has a refund provision. Only 11056 cl.(4) addresses refunds.

(c) P became dutiable 7 days after signing (Sep 8 to Sep 15). S became dutiable 7 days after signing (Oct 23 to Oct 30). The preambles of the scope proclamations recite the 30-day rule (¶8 in 11064 and 11065, ¶9 in 11076). Their operative text does not explain how a 7-day lag fits it.
Q5.uncertainty: Whether the 30-day rule applies to scope changes is not addressed. The most defensible reading is that the 30 days ran for the original duty and the later changes modify an existing action. Products on the Part lists cannot be read, so the scenarios are taken as given.

Q6.answer:
(a) The column shows: Section 301 duty / MFN duty at 4% / total. Value is $100,000.
1. Switzerland: 12.5% net of MFN. (12.5% − 4%) = 8.5% × $100,000 = $8,500 / $4,000 / $12,500.
2. Norway: flat 12.5% × $100,000 = $12,500 / $4,000 / $16,500.
3. United Kingdom: flat 10% × $100,000 = $10,000 / $4,000 / $14,000.
4. Germany (EU): 10% net of MFN. (10% − 4%) = 6% × $100,000 = $6,000 / $4,000 / $10,000.
5. Taiwan: 10% net of MFN, so $6,000 / $4,000 / $10,000.
6. Türkiye: flat 12.5%, so $12,500 / $4,000 / $16,500.
7. Japan: 12.5% net of MFN, so $8,500 / $4,000 / $12,500.
8. Liechtenstein: it is not one of the 60 investigated economies. The documents contain no rule treating it as Swiss, so I find no section 301 duty: $0 / $4,000 / $4,000.
9. Hong Kong: flat 12.5%, so $12,500 / $4,000 / $16,500.
10. India: flat 10%, so $10,000 / $4,000 / $14,000.

(b) Section 301 duty only, on $100,000:
- Germany, MFN 12%: 12% is at least 10%, so $0.
- Japan, MFN 12%: (12.5% − 12%) = 0.5% × $100,000 = $500.
- Taiwan, MFN exactly 10%: $0.
- South Korea, MFN exactly 10%: (12.5% − 10%) = 2.5% × $100,000 = $2,500.
- Switzerland, MFN free: 12.5% × $100,000 = $12,500.

(c) The treatment differs from the June proposal for five of the ten economies.
- Switzerland and Japan: proposed at flat 12.5%, adopted at 12.5% net of MFN.
- Germany (the EU) and Taiwan: proposed at flat 10%, adopted at 10% net of MFN.
- India: the rate itself changed from 12.5% to 10%. The stated reason is India's 'adoption of a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN'.
- Norway, the UK, Türkiye and Hong Kong are unchanged. Liechtenstein was not covered in either document.
Q6.basis: Memo (FR Doc. 2026-15274) sec. 1(a)(i)-(iii), 91 FR 47720. Notice (2026-15181): II.A at 47320-47321. EU at 47323, India at 47324, Hong Kong at 47323, Switzerland at 47327, Taiwan at 47327, Türkiye at 47328, UK at 47328. Proposal (2026-11296) Part IV at 91 FR 34274. Section 301 stacks on MFN under U.S. note 52(a), 91 FR 47352.
Q6.uncertainty: Liechtenstein's treatment, for example under any customs-union rule, is not addressed in the readable text. Annex exemption lists are images and are assumed not to cover the product.

Q7.answer:
(a) France is an EU member state, so the 10% net-of-MFN cap applies. Column 1 duty = $0.03 × 2,000 kg = $60. Ad valorem equivalent = $60 / $12,000 = 0.5%. Section 301 rate = 10% − 0.5% = 9.5%. Section 301 duty = 9.5% × $12,000 = $1,140.

(b) Column 1 duty = 4% × $20,000 = $800, plus $0.25 × 4,000 kg = $1,000, for $1,800. Ad valorem equivalent = $1,800 / $20,000 = 9%.
- Italy (cap 10%): (10% − 9%) = 1% × $20,000 = $200.
- Japan (cap 12.5%): (12.5% − 9%) = 3.5% × $20,000 = $700.
- Brazil: the net-of-MFN rule does not cover Brazil, so a flat 12.5% × $20,000 = $2,500.

(c) The ad valorem equivalent is $2,200 / $20,000 = 11%.
- Taiwan (cap 10%): 11% is at least 10%, so $0.
- Switzerland (cap 12.5%): (12.5% − 11%) = 1.5% × $20,000 = $300.

(d) The rule for non-ad valorem rates is in U.S. note 52(k), subdivision (k), at 91 FR 47394. It covers members of the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan. The ad valorem equivalent is the column 1-General duty payable divided by the customs value. Its closing paragraphs state the sums for rates below the cap: for headings 9903.05.39 and .76 the sum is 10%, and for .49, .71 and .74 it is 12.5%. The result for an equivalent at or above the cap (section 301 duty of zero) is stated in the Memo sec. 1(a)(ii) at 91 FR 47320 and in the Notice at 47320-47321, and in the economy paragraphs for the EU (47323), Korea (47327), Switzerland (47327) and Taiwan (47327).
Q7.uncertainty: The heading descriptions that may repeat the zero-result rule are images. Note (k) applies to Japan, Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan and EU states, so Brazil takes the flat rate.

Q8.answer:
(a) The Dominican Republic rate is a flat 12.5%. 12.5% × $80,000 = $10,000 where the duty applies.
1. Loaded on a vessel Jul 22 and entered Jul 29: the transit exception needs entry before 12:01 a.m. Jul 28. Duty owed: $10,000.
2. Entered 3:00 p.m. Jul 27: the vessel was loaded before 12:01 a.m. Jul 24 and entry was before 12:01 a.m. Jul 28, so the exception applies. Duty owed: $0.
3. Entered 12:01 a.m. Jul 28: that is not 'before' 12:01 a.m. Jul 28. Duty owed: $10,000.
4. Loaded 6:00 a.m. Jul 24: loading was after the cutoff, so the exception does not apply. Duty owed: $10,000.
5. Entered Jul 23: before the 12:01 a.m. Jul 24 start. Duty owed: $0.
6. Bonded warehouse withdrawal Jul 26: this is a withdrawal after the start, and warehoused goods were not loaded on a vessel and in transit. Duty owed: $10,000.
7. Air freight: the exception names only 'a vessel'. The text is silent on aircraft, so on the text the duty applies: $10,000.

(b) The transit rule is stated only in the DATES paragraph of the Notice (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318). It covers 'goods loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in transit on the final mode of transit before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 24, 2026, and entered ... or withdrawn ... before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 28, 2026'.

(c) The presidential memorandum was signed Jul 23, 2026. The duties apply from 12:01 a.m. ET Jul 24, 2026, for goods entered or withdrawn for consumption on or after that time. Both the Notice (91 FR 47318) and the Memorandum (91 FR 47717) were published Jul 28, 2026.

(d) Patented pharmaceutical article under heading 9903.04.62:
- Entered Jul 30: the exemption starts Jul 31, so 12.5% × $80,000 = $10,000.
- Entered Aug 3: exempt under note 52(f)(8), so $0.
Q8.basis: Notice (2026-15181): DATES at 91 FR 47318. Rate for the Dominican Republic at 47323. Annex I.B (patented pharmaceuticals, effective 12:01 a.m. Jul 31, adds item (8) to note 52(f)) at 47394. Memo (2026-15274), published 91 FR 47717.
Q8.uncertainty: Air shipments are not covered by the transit text. Annex II Part A and product lists are images and are assumed not to cover the goods.

Q9.answer:
(a) Thailand (12.5%), heading 9802.00.80: the duty applies to the assembled article's value less the cost or value of the U.S. products. ($100,000 − $35,000) = $65,000 × 12.5% = $8,125.
(b) Israel (12.5%), subheading 9802.00.50: the duty applies to the value of the repairs. $6,000 × 12.5% = $750.
(c) Mexico (10%): (i) entered free under the USMCA: exempt under note 52(h), so $0. (ii) no USMCA claim: 10% × $50,000 = $5,000. The MFN 5% is a separate layer.
(d) Japanese passenger car under heading 9903.94.01: exempt under note 52(f)(2), so $0.
(e) Brazil (12.5%) with a section 232 duty under a chapter 99 heading the note does not list: no readable exemption, so 12.5% × $100,000 = $12,500.
(f) The June proposal said the exemptions would include informational materials (for example, books), donations, accompanied baggage and 'all articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs'. The adopted text exempts only listed section 232 headings (note 52(f)), and baggage items for personal use (note 52(a)). It contains no readable informational-materials or donations exemption.
Q9.basis: Notice (2026-15181): note 52(a) at 91 FR 47352; note 52(f) at 47362-63; notes 52(g)-(h) at 47363; rates in II.B at 47321-47328. Proposal (2026-11296) at 91 FR 34274. Notice recital at 47318.
Q9.uncertainty: Annex II Part A and the headings 9903.05.85 onward are images, and informational materials or donations may be exempted there. The Brazil answer assumes no list covers the unmentioned 232 heading.

Q10.answer:
Scenario 1 (aluminum extrusions, $200,000, MFN 3%):
(a) Sep 10, 2026:
- MFN: 3% × $200,000 = $6,000.
- Section 232: 50% × $200,000 = $100,000.
- Section 338: $0, because the original proclamation excludes 232 articles and the scope change starts Sep 15.
- Section 301: $0. Canada is at 10% but heading 9903.82.02 articles are exempt under note 52(f)(1).
- Total: $106,000.
(b) Sep 16, 2026:
- MFN: $6,000.
- Section 232: $100,000.
- Section 338: 50% × $200,000 = $100,000 (11065 cl.(1) makes the duty apply in addition to section 232).
- Section 301: $0.
- Total: $206,000.

Scenario 2 (rye whisky, $60,000, MFN free):
(c) Sep 1, USMCA free: section 338 = 50% × $60,000 = $30,000 (no USMCA exemption in the readable 338 text). Section 301 = $0 (note 52(g)). Total $30,000.
(d) Sep 1, no USMCA claim: section 338 = $30,000. Section 301 = 10% × $60,000 = $6,000. Total $36,000.
(e) Arrives Oct 2: it is excluded from importation (imported after 12:01 a.m. Sep 29), so no entry is possible and no duty is owed. Section 338 = $0, section 301 = $0, total $0. If the ban were invalidated, the 50% duty would apply under 11061 cl.(9)(b): $30,000, plus $6,000 of section 301 if no USMCA claim.

(f) Neither the IEEPA Canada duties nor the 10% surcharge applied to Canadian goods entered in September 2026.
- IEEPA: EO 14389 (signed Feb 20, published Feb 25, 2026, 91 FR 9437) says the IEEPA duties under EO 14193 and others 'shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as practicable, shall no longer be collected'.
- Surcharge: Proclamation 11012 (91 FR 9339) imposed 10% for 150 days from Feb 24, 2026, through 12:01 a.m. EDT Jul 24, 2026. It also excluded section 232 articles and USMCA goods. No extension was found.
- What does apply to Canada in September: the section 301 10% duty (non-USMCA) and the section 338 duties.
Q10.uncertainty: I assumed no USMCA exemption in the 338 proclamations beyond what is readable. EO 14389 has no stated effective time. The section 301 exemptions and annexes are images.

Q11.answer:
Discrepancies found:
1. Textile mechanism. The Memo recital says USTR 'proposed to establish a textile mechanism that would allow a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to enter ... at a zero section 301 tariff rate' (Memo, 91 FR 47719). The June proposal says the volume would enter 'at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate' (June FRN, 91 FR 34274).
2. Cambodia and Guatemala. The Memo (91 FR 47720) and the Notice (47319) name Cambodia and Guatemala among economies that adopted bans after the proposal, and the Memo says their goods 'should be tariffed at the 10 percent rate'. The June proposal already placed both at 10% (June FRN, 34274), so their rate did not change.
3. Section 232 exemption. The Notice (47330) says USTR exempted 'all of the products proposed for exemption in Annex A ... except the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products', and the June proposal exempted 'all articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs' (34274). The adopted note 52(f) (47362-63) exempts only enumerated 232 headings.
4. Start date. 11056 cl.(1) sets the effective date at Aug 22 (91 FR 54790). Later recitals describe 11046, 11047 and 11048 as imposing duties 'effective August 19, 2026' (11061 ¶1 at 58311; 11064 ¶1 at 58331; 11065 ¶1 at 58339; 11076 ¶1 at 68861). The clauses of the original proclamations were not amended (46641).
5. Suspension versus new date. 11056 is titled a 'temporary suspension', speaks of 'suspending for a period of 3 days' (¶4-5, 54790) and directs agencies to 'suspend the collection' (cl.(2)). Its operative cl.(1) sets a new effective date and has no lapse mechanism. 11061 ¶4 (58311) says 'the 3-day suspension imposed by Proclamation 11056 lapsed'.
6. Alcohol finding. 11056 ¶1 (54789), 11061 ¶1 (58311) and 11064 ¶1 (58331) say 11046 found Canada's imposition 'is not equally enforced upon the like articles of every foreign country'. 11046 ¶7 (46640) makes findings of unreasonable limitation, discrimination in fact, burden and disadvantage, but not that one. The dairy and motor-vehicles proclamations do make it (46654, 46664).
7. Missing dairy scope proclamation. 11062 cl.(3) (58320) refers to a 'Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope ... With Respect to Dairy)'. No such document was found. Only alcohol (11064) and motor-vehicles (11065) scope proclamations exist.
8. Determinations. Both the June FRN (34274) and the Notice (47319) say 'all of the investigated economies have failed both to impose ... and to effectively enforce' a prohibition. The same passages say six economies (Canada, Ecuador, the EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan) only failed to enforce one they have.

Not listed, because the documents are silent or the matter is an image: whether the 30-day rule fits the 7-day scope changes; the list contents.
Q11.uncertainty: The list may be incomplete: preambles of the economy sections of the Notice and annexes were read only selectively. Items 3 and 5 turn on the reading of the operative text. Item 3 may be affected by image annexes.

Q12.answer:
All entries Sep 10, 2026. Exemptions are the per-economy lists in note 52. Rates: Cambodia 10%, Malaysia 10%, Taiwan 10% net of MFN, Bangladesh 10%, Argentina 10%, Japan 12.5% net of MFN, Indonesia 10%, Mexico 10%, Thailand 12.5%, El Salvador 10%, Italy (EU) 10% net of MFN.
(a) Aloe etc. (1302.19.91), $60,000: Cambodia $0 (exempt, note 52(j)(5)(ii)(C)). Malaysia: its list has no aloe, so 10% × $60,000 = $6,000.
(b) Boswellia (1301.90.91), $100,000: Malaysia $0 (exempt). Taiwan $0 (exempt). Bangladesh: not listed, so 10% × $100,000 = $10,000. Argentina: not listed, so $10,000.
(c) Argan oil (1515.90.81), $100,000, MFN 4%: Taiwan $0 (exempt). Japan: (12.5% − 4%) = 8.5% × $100,000 = $8,500. Indonesia: its list has only aloe, so 10% × $100,000 = $10,000.
(d) Sesame seeds for sowing (1207.40.00): exempt for every economy under note 52(c)(4), so Japan, Mexico and Thailand each owe $0.
(e) Psyllium husks (1211.90.89), $40,000: Cambodia $0 (exempt). Thailand: 12.5% × $40,000 = $5,000. El Salvador: its list has only aloe, so 10% × $40,000 = $4,000. Italy, MFN 2%: (10% − 2%) = 8% × $40,000 = $3,200.
Q12.basis: Notice (2026-15181), U.S. note 52(c)(4) at 91 FR 47356; Malaysia (j)(4)(ii) at 47365; Cambodia (j)(5)(ii) at 47366; El Salvador (j)(7)(ii) at 47375; Argentina (j)(8)(ii) at 47383; Bangladesh (j)(9)(ii) at 47383; Taiwan (j)(10)(ii) at 47384; Indonesia (j)(11)(ii) at 47385; net-of-MFN rule at 47320. Rates in II.B at 47321-47328.
Q12.uncertainty: Each economy also has image lists of exempt headings (Annex II Parts and note 52(j)(i)). I assumed none covers these goods, as the scenarios state.

Q13.answer:
The rates come from Proc. 11032 cl.(2), which applies to entries from Jun 8, 2026 through 11:59 p.m. EST Dec 31, 2027. Section 232 duty only:
(a) Canada, USMCA claim, U.S. parts $60,000: 25% applies only to the non-U.S. content, ($200,000 − $60,000) = $140,000 × 25% = $35,000. That is 17.5% of value, above the 15% floor, so $35,000.
(b) Canada, USMCA claim, no U.S. content: 25% × $200,000 = $50,000.
(c) Canada, no USMCA: cl.(2)(a) 25% × $200,000 = $50,000. The U.S.-content rule in cl.(2)(d) applies only to USMCA-qualifying goods.
(d) Japan, MFN 2.5%: the sum of the column 1 duty and 232 is 15%, so (15% − 2.5%) = 12.5% × $200,000 = $25,000.
(e) Canada, USMCA claim, U.S. parts $20,000 and $30,000 of U.S.-cast aluminum in a Canadian part: only 'parts produced in the United States' count, so non-U.S. content = ($200,000 − $20,000) = $180,000 × 25% = $45,000 (22.5%, above the floor).
(f) The same unit entered Oct 6, 2026: also $45,000. I found no document that changes the rule between Oct 6 and Oct 20.
(g) U.S. parts $140,000: non-U.S. content ($200,000 − $140,000) = $60,000 × 25% = $15,000, which is 7.5% of value. The total effective duty may not be less than 15%, so 15% × $200,000 = $30,000.
(h) The (a) treatment runs until 11:59 p.m. EST Dec 31, 2027. From 12:01 a.m. EST Jan 1, 2028 the rates are those in clause (3) of Proclamation 11021: 25%, or 15% for qualifying U.K. goods and 10% where the metal is wholly U.S.-melted or U.S.-cast. That clause has no USMCA content rule, so 25% × $200,000 = $50,000 would be owed.
Q13.uncertainty: Whether U.S.-cast aluminum in a Canadian-made part earns any credit under cl.(2)(d) is not addressed. If $30,000 were credited, the duty in (e) would be $37,500. Annex IV (image) and any CBP guidance on 'U.S. content' were not available. Whether the full-value rule applies after 2027 is inferred from clause (3).

Q14.answer:
1. Incorrect. The Memo recital says only that USTR informed the President the TRQs will be feasible 'by September 1, 2026'. Sec. 2 says 'as soon as the Trade Representative determines that it is feasible', and the Notice says 'when feasible'. There is no deadline.
2. Incorrect. USTR received over 1,600 written comments and over 100 witnesses testified over three days.
3. Partly correct. Seven economies are named as having acted after the proposal: six adopted bans (Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago) and Jordan undertook an ART commitment. Only five moved from 12.5% to 10%: Honduras, India, Jordan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago. Cambodia and Guatemala were already at 10% in the proposal.
4. Incorrect. Commenters opposed exempting beef and avocados, and USTR 'determined not to remove these products from the list of exempted products'.
5. Incorrect. The net-of-MFN economies are the EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea and Switzerland. Japan and Korea have only Annex II Part A, not their own list. Only the EU (Part C), Switzerland (Part D) and Taiwan (Part K) have one.
6. Partly correct. USTR added 471 products to the exemption list, but the Notice says 'certain sugar and sugar containing products', not all.
7. Incorrect. The total-duty cap applies only to net-of-MFN economies: 10% for the EU and Taiwan, and 12.5% for Japan, Korea and Switzerland. Other economies owe the section 301 rate on top of MFN.
8. Correct. Products admitted to a U.S. foreign trade zone may be admitted only in privileged foreign status once the duty is imposed, unless eligible for domestic status under 19 CFR 146.43.
9. Correct. If an exemption is held invalid, only that exemption or part is invalid, and the tariff applies to imports to which the invalidated exemption applied. That is the Notice's severability section and Memo sec. 4(e).
10. Correct per the Notice, which says USTR exempted all Annex A products except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals. Caveat: the adopted section 232 exemption in note 52(f) is limited to enumerated headings.
Q14.basis: Memo (2026-15274): 91 FR 47719-20, sec. 1-2 at 47720-47721, sec. 4(e) at 47722-23. Notice (2026-15181): 47318, 47319 (comments and witnesses; the seven economies), 47320-47321, 47321 (FTZ), 47330-47331 (beef, avocados, chemicals; 471 products; sugar), 47335 (severability). Per-economy lists at 47321-47328.
Q14.uncertainty: Annex II Part lists are images. Statement 3 depends on how 'moved' is read. Statement 10 depends on whether the section 232 point counts as a cut-back.

Q15.answer:
Assume a $100,000 customs value, all aluminum, MFN excluded. Amounts are by authority. Case N = no USMCA. Case U = USMCA claim.
1. Feb 10, 2025: IEEPA Canada 25% was paused until Mar 4. 232: the Canada exemption ended Mar 12, 2025. Total N: $0. U: $0.
2. Mar 6, 2025: IEEPA 25% in force. USMCA goods were exempt only from Mar 7. 232 not yet. N: $25,000. U: $25,000.
3. Mar 10, 2025: N: IEEPA 25% = $25,000. U: IEEPA $0 (USMCA exempt since Mar 7). 232 not yet. N: $25,000. U: $0.
4. Mar 14, 2025: 232 aluminum at 25% since Mar 12 = $25,000. IEEPA stacks (N: +$25,000; U: $0). N: $50,000. U: $25,000.
5. Jun 3, 2025: same as Mar 14 (232 still 25%). N: $50,000. U: $25,000.
6. Jun 10, 2025: 232 at 50% from Jun 4 = $50,000. IEEPA N +$25,000. N: $75,000. U: $50,000.
7. Aug 5, 2025: 232 $50,000. IEEPA at 35% from Aug 1 (N: $35,000). N: $85,000. U: $50,000.
8. Mar 2, 2026: 232 $50,000. IEEPA ended (EO 14389). Section 122 10% not owed because 232 articles are excluded and USMCA goods are excluded. N and U: $50,000.
9. Jun 10, 2026: 232 at 50% (Annex I-A) = $50,000. Section 122 not owed (232). N and U: $50,000.
10. Jul 27, 2026: 232 $50,000. Section 122 expired Jul 24. Section 301 Canada 10% from Jul 24: not owed (note 52(f)(1)). Section 338 not yet in force. N and U: $50,000.
11. Aug 25, 2026: 232 $50,000. Section 338 in force from Aug 22 but cl.(2) excludes 232 articles: $0. Section 301 not owed. N and U: $50,000.
12. Sep 14, 2026: same as Aug 25. N and U: $50,000.
13. Sep 16, 2026: 232 $50,000. Section 338 50% = $50,000 (11065 cl.(1)). Section 301 not owed. N and U: $100,000.
14. Nov 10, 2026: same as Sep 16. N and U: $100,000.
Reciprocal tariffs (EO 14257) are not owed in 2025, because 232 aluminum articles and Canadian goods are excluded.
Q15.uncertainty: The stacking of IEEPA Canada duties on 232 aluminum is read from EO 14193's 'in addition' clause and the absence of any exemption in the documents found. The 232 rates for Mar 12 and Jun 3, 2025 come from the signing proclamation text only partially read. Whether the 338 duty applies to USMCA goods depends on Annex I exceptions, which are images. EO 14389 states no effective time.
